before.content_html:
The Reactivity Series

Metals can be arranged in order of their reactivity series. The most reactive metals (such as potassium and sodium) are at the top, and the least reactive (such as gold and platinum) are at the bottom. The reactivity of a metal depends on how easily it forms a positive ion by losing its outer-shell electrons. Metals higher in the series lose electrons more readily because their outer electrons are further from the nucleus and more shielded by inner electron shells.

The order from most to least reactive is: potassium, sodium, lithium, calcium, magnesium, aluminium, carbon, zinc, iron, hydrogen, copper, silver, gold, platinum. Carbon and hydrogen are included as reference points even though they are not metals — carbon’s position determines how metals can be extracted, and hydrogen’s position determines which metals react with dilute acids.

Key Fact

A metal’s reactivity depends on how easily it loses its outer electrons to form a positive ion. More reactive metals react more vigorously with water and dilute acids. The tendency to form positive ions increases up the reactivity series.

Reactions of Metals

You can deduce the reactivity of a metal from its reactions with water and dilute acids. Very reactive metals (K, Na, Li, Ca) react vigorously with cold water to produce a metal hydroxide and hydrogen gas. For example, sodium reacts with water: \(2Na(s) + 2H_2O(l) \rightarrow 2NaOH(aq) + H_2(g)\). Calcium reacts more gently, producing a cloudy solution as calcium hydroxide is only slightly soluble.

Moderately reactive metals (Mg, Zn, Fe) react very slowly or not at all with cold water but react well with dilute acids to produce a salt and hydrogen gas. For example, magnesium reacts with hydrochloric acid: \(Mg(s) + 2HCl(aq) \rightarrow MgCl_2(aq) + H_2(g)\). Unreactive metals (Cu, Ag, Au) do not react with water or dilute acids because they do not lose their electrons easily enough.

Displacement Reactions

A displacement reaction occurs when a more reactive metal replaces a less reactive metal from a compound. For example, if you place iron in copper sulfate solution, the iron displaces the copper:

$$Fe(s) + CuSO_4(aq) \rightarrow FeSO_4(aq) + Cu(s)$$

The iron is more reactive than copper, so it displaces it. The blue copper sulfate solution turns colourless (iron sulfate) and a brown coating of copper appears on the iron. A less reactive metal cannot displace a more reactive one — copper in iron sulfate solution would show no reaction. This principle can be applied to any pair of metals: if the added metal is higher in the reactivity series than the metal in the salt, displacement occurs.

You can work out a reactivity order by doing a series of displacement experiments. Place different metals into solutions of other metal salts. If a displacement occurs (colour change, solid deposited, temperature rise), the added metal is more reactive. If nothing happens, the added metal is less reactive. By testing several combinations systematically, you can rank the metals in order of reactivity. You can also compare how vigorously different metals react with dilute acid — faster fizzing and more heat indicates higher reactivity.

Extracting Metals

How a metal is extracted from its ore depends on its position in the reactivity series. Metals below carbon in the series (such as iron, zinc and copper) can be extracted by reduction with carbon. The carbon is more reactive, so it displaces the metal from its oxide and takes the oxygen. For example, extracting iron from iron oxide:

$$2Fe_2O_3 + 3C \rightarrow 4Fe + 3CO_2$$

In this reaction, the iron oxide is reduced (loses oxygen) and the carbon is oxidised (gains oxygen). This is why carbon reduction is also a redox reaction. Metals above carbon in the series (such as aluminium, sodium and potassium) are too reactive to be extracted by carbon. They must be extracted by electrolysis, which is more expensive because it uses large amounts of electricity. For example, aluminium is extracted from aluminium oxide (bauxite) by electrolysis at around 960°C.

Biological methods offer alternatives to traditional extraction, particularly for low-grade ores where conventional mining is not economically viable. Phytoextraction uses plants to absorb metal compounds from the soil through their roots; the plants are harvested and burned, and the metal is extracted from the ash. Bioleaching uses bacteria to produce acidic solutions that dissolve metal compounds from the ore; the metal can then be extracted from the solution by displacement or electrolysis. These methods are slower but have lower environmental impact and can extract metals from ores that would otherwise be waste.

Key Fact

Metals below carbon in the reactivity series are extracted by reduction with carbon (heating the oxide with carbon). Metals above carbon must be extracted by electrolysis. The choice of method depends entirely on the metal’s reactivity relative to carbon.
before.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The reactivity series ranks metals by how easily they form positive ions. More reactive metals react more vigorously with water and acids.
  • A more reactive metal displaces a less reactive metal from a compound. Displacement experiments can be used to deduce a reactivity order.
  • Metals below carbon are extracted by reduction with carbon. Metals above carbon require electrolysis. Biological methods (phytoextraction, bioleaching) are alternatives.

practice_questions.text: Iron is extracted from iron oxide in a blast furnace by heating with carbon. Copper can also be extracted by heating copper oxide with carbon. However, titanium cannot be extracted this way. Discuss the principles of metal extraction, explaining why different methods are needed for different metals.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (5-6): Comprehensive discussion covering the reactivity series, position of carbon, reduction with carbon for Fe and Cu, electrolysis for metals above carbon, with balanced equations or examples.
Mid band (3-4): Explains the principle with reference to the reactivity series but may lack examples or detail.
Lower band (1-2): Basic statement about reactivity.
Indicative content:
• The method of extraction depends on the metal’s position in the reactivity series.
• Carbon is in the middle of the series.
• Iron and copper are below carbon, so they can be reduced by carbon (e.g. 2Fe₂O₃ + 3C → 4Fe + 3CO₂).
• Carbon displaces the less reactive metal from its oxide.
• Titanium is above carbon / too reactive for carbon reduction.
• Metals above carbon must be extracted by electrolysis (more expensive).
• Biological methods (phytoextraction, bioleaching) are alternatives for low-grade ores.

before.content_html:
Why We Need Chemical Tests

Chemists often need to identify unknown substances. This might be to check whether a water supply is safe, to identify minerals in rocks, to verify the purity of a manufactured product, or to analyse an unknown sample in a forensic investigation. The OCR Gateway specification requires you to know several key tests that can identify specific ions and gases. These tests fall into two broad categories: traditional wet chemistry tests that rely on visible observations, and modern instrumental methods that use machines for faster, more accurate results.

Flame Tests

A flame test identifies metal ions by the colour they produce when heated in a Bunsen burner flame. Different metal ions emit light of different colours because their electrons absorb energy and then release it as visible light at characteristic wavelengths. To carry out a flame test: dip a clean nichrome wire loop in concentrated hydrochloric acid (to remove previous residues), then dip it into the sample, and hold it in a blue Bunsen flame. The wire must be cleaned thoroughly between tests to avoid contamination from previous samples, which would give misleading results.

Key Fact

Flame test colours: Lithium — crimson red. Sodium — yellow. Potassium — lilac. Calcium — orange-red. Copper — green / blue-green.

Tests for Gases

You must be able to test for four gases. Each test produces a unique, easily identifiable result:

Hydrogen (\(H_2\)) — hold a burning splint near the mouth of the test tube; a squeaky pop confirms hydrogen. The pop is caused by the hydrogen igniting and reacting with oxygen in the air: \(2H_2 + O_2 \rightarrow 2H_2O\). Oxygen (\(O_2\)) — insert a glowing splint into the gas; it relights because oxygen supports combustion. Carbon dioxide (\(CO_2\)) — bubble the gas through limewater (calcium hydroxide solution); it turns milky or cloudy because insoluble calcium carbonate is formed: \(Ca(OH)_2 + CO_2 \rightarrow CaCO_3 + H_2O\). Chlorine (\(Cl_2\)) — hold damp litmus paper near the gas; it is first turned red (because chlorine is acidic) and then bleached white because chlorine is a powerful bleaching agent.

Testing for Metal Ions Using Sodium Hydroxide

Adding sodium hydroxide solution (NaOH) to solutions containing metal ions produces coloured precipitates. The precipitate forms because the metal ions react with hydroxide ions to produce an insoluble metal hydroxide. The colour of the precipitate identifies the metal ion present. This is a key practical skill for the exam.

Calcium ions (\(Ca^{2+}\)) — white precipitate of calcium hydroxide. Copper(II) ions (\(Cu^{2+}\)) — blue precipitate of copper hydroxide. Iron(II) ions (\(Fe^{2+}\)) — green precipitate of iron(II) hydroxide; the equation is \(Fe^{2+} + 2OH^- \rightarrow Fe(OH)_2\). Iron(III) ions (\(Fe^{3+}\)) — brown precipitate of iron(III) hydroxide; the equation is \(Fe^{3+} + 3OH^- \rightarrow Fe(OH)_3\). Aluminium ions (\(Al^{3+}\)) — white precipitate that dissolves in excess NaOH to form a colourless solution (aluminium hydroxide is amphoteric). Magnesium ions (\(Mg^{2+}\)) — white precipitate that does not dissolve in excess NaOH. This difference between aluminium and magnesium is important: both give white precipitates, but only aluminium’s dissolves in excess.

Testing for Negative Ions

You can test for certain negative ions (anions) using specific reagents:

Carbonate ions (\(CO_3^{2-}\)) — add dilute acid (such as hydrochloric acid) to the sample. If carbonates are present, the acid reacts to produce carbon dioxide gas, which can be tested by bubbling it through limewater — it turns milky if \(CO_2\) is present. Sulfate ions (\(SO_4^{2-}\)) — first add dilute hydrochloric acid to remove any carbonate ions that might interfere, then add barium chloride solution. A white precipitate of barium sulfate (\(BaSO_4\)) confirms sulfate ions are present. Halide ions — first add dilute nitric acid (to remove other ions that might interfere), then add silver nitrate solution. Chloride ions (\(Cl^-\)) give a white precipitate of silver chloride, bromide ions (\(Br^-\)) give a cream precipitate of silver bromide, and iodide ions (\(I^-\)) give a yellow precipitate of silver iodide.

Key Fact

Halide tests with silver nitrate: chloride \(\rightarrow\) white precipitate, bromide \(\rightarrow\) cream precipitate, iodide \(\rightarrow\) yellow precipitate. Always acidify with dilute nitric acid first to prevent interference from other ions.

When identifying an unknown ionic compound, work systematically. First dissolve the sample in water. Use a flame test to identify the metal ion (cation). Then use precipitate tests with NaOH to confirm the metal ion. Next, test for the negative ion (anion) using the appropriate reagent — silver nitrate for halides, barium chloride for sulfates, or dilute acid for carbonates. Record all observations carefully and compare with known results.

Instrumental Methods

Instrumental methods of analysis are faster, more sensitive and more accurate than traditional chemical tests. Gas chromatography separates the components of a mixture by passing it through a column; each component travels at a different rate, producing separate peaks on a chromatogram. The number of peaks tells you how many components are in the mixture, and the retention time identifies each substance. Mass spectrometry gives the relative molecular mass of a substance by measuring the mass-to-charge ratio of its ions. Gas chromatography linked with mass spectrometry (GC-MS) is particularly powerful because it both separates and identifies components in a single analysis. These methods are used in forensic science, environmental monitoring, drug testing and the pharmaceutical industry.

Instrumental methods can detect very small quantities of a substance (high sensitivity), making them invaluable when only a trace amount is available. They are fast and can be automated for processing many samples. They give accurate, quantitative results rather than just qualitative observations. However, the equipment is expensive to purchase and maintain, and requires trained operators to interpret the data correctly. Despite these costs, instrumental analysis has largely replaced traditional tests in professional laboratories.

practice_questions.text: State what is meant by dynamic equilibrium.
practice_questions.marks:
Award 1 mark:
• When the rate of the forward reaction equals the rate of the reverse reaction (in a closed system) / concentrations of reactants and products are constant (1).

practice_questions.text: Describe what the symbol \(\rightleftharpoons\) means in a chemical equation.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks:
• The reaction is reversible (1).
• It can proceed in both the forward and reverse directions (1).

practice_questions.text: Explain the effect of increasing pressure on the equilibrium position of the Haber process reaction: \(N_2(g) + 3H_2(g) \rightleftharpoons 2NH_3(g)\).
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 3 marks:
• Increasing pressure shifts the equilibrium to the right / towards products (1).
• Because the product side has fewer gas molecules (2 vs 4) (1).
• This opposes the increase in pressure / Le Chatelier’s principle (1).

practice_questions.text: The forward reaction of the Haber process is exothermic. A factory manager suggests lowering the temperature to 200°C to increase the yield of ammonia. Compare the advantages and disadvantages of this suggestion.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks:
• Lower temperature would increase the yield / shift equilibrium to the right (exothermic direction favoured) (1).
• However, lower temperature means a slower rate of reaction (1).
• It would take much longer to reach equilibrium (1).
• The actual temperature (~450°C) is a compromise between yield and rate (1).

practice_questions.text: Describe the role of the iron catalyst in the Haber process.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks:
• It speeds up both the forward and reverse reactions / helps equilibrium be reached faster (1).
• It does not change the position of equilibrium / does not change the yield (1).

practice_questions.text: The industrial conditions for the Haber process are described as a compromise. Discuss how temperature, pressure and the use of a catalyst are chosen to maximise efficiency and economic viability. Use Le Chatelier’s principle in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (5-6): Comprehensive discussion covering all three factors with Le Chatelier’s reasoning, the compromise concept, and economic considerations.
Mid band (3-4): Discusses two factors with some Le Chatelier’s reasoning.
Lower band (1-2): Basic statements about one or two factors.
Indicative content:
• Forward reaction is exothermic; low temperature favours products (Le Chatelier).
• But low temperature → slow rate, so ~450°C is used as a compromise.
• 4 moles of gas on left, 2 on right; high pressure favours products.
• High pressure is expensive (strong equipment, energy costs), so ~200 atm is used.
• Iron catalyst speeds up both reactions equally; equilibrium reached faster.
• Catalyst does not change yield but reduces time and energy costs.
• Unreacted N₂ and H₂ are recycled.

before.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Reversible reactions can go in both directions. Dynamic equilibrium is reached in a closed system when the forward and reverse rates are equal.
  • Le Chatelier’s principle: changing temperature, concentration or pressure shifts the equilibrium to oppose the change. Catalysts do not change the equilibrium position.
  • The Haber process makes ammonia at ~450°C, ~200 atm with an iron catalyst — a compromise between yield and rate.
before.exam_tip_html: When applying Le Chatelier’s principle, state the change, the direction the equilibrium shifts, and why (to oppose the change). For the Haber process, always explain that the conditions are a compromise — the word “compromise” is essential for full marks. Remember: a catalyst does not shift the equilibrium position.

before.description: Metal extraction, life cycle assessments, crude oil fractions and cracking.
before.content_html:
Atom Economy and Percentage Yield

In industrial chemistry, it is not enough to simply make a product — the process must be efficient and produce as little waste as possible. Two key measures of efficiency are atom economy and percentage yield.

Atom economy measures how much of the mass of the reactants ends up as the useful product. A high atom economy means less waste is produced, which is better for both the environment and the company’s costs. It is calculated using:

$$\text{atom economy} = \frac{M_r \text{ of desired product}}{\text{sum of } M_r \text{ of all products}} \times 100$$

Percentage yield compares the actual amount of product obtained to the maximum theoretical amount (from the balanced equation):

$$\text{percentage yield} = \frac{\text{actual yield}}{\text{theoretical yield}} \times 100$$

Percentage yield is often less than 100% because of incomplete reactions, side reactions, product lost during purification, or reversible reactions that do not go to completion. The limiting reactant is the one that runs out first and determines the maximum amount of product that can be formed. The other reactant is said to be in excess — some of it will be left over when the reaction finishes. For example, if you react 2 g of magnesium with 100 cm³ of excess hydrochloric acid, the magnesium is the limiting reactant and determines how much hydrogen is produced.

Key Fact

Atom economy measures the proportion of reactant atoms that become the desired product. Percentage yield measures how much product was actually made compared to the theoretical maximum. Both should be as high as possible for economic and environmental reasons. Industry aims for reactions with 100% atom economy (where all atoms end up in the desired product), but this is not always achievable, especially in reactions that produce by-products.

Life Cycle Assessments

A life cycle assessment (LCA) evaluates the environmental impact of a product at every stage of its life. The four main stages are: (1) extracting and processing raw materials, (2) manufacturing the product, (3) using the product (including transport), and (4) disposing of the product at the end of its life.

LCAs consider: energy consumption at each stage, raw material use, water use, emissions to air (including greenhouse gases), emissions to water, waste produced, and the potential for recycling or reuse. However, some aspects are difficult to quantify (e.g. the impact of noise pollution or visual impact), which makes LCAs partly subjective. Different analysts may reach different conclusions depending on the weighting they give to different factors. Companies may also use LCAs selectively to support marketing claims, so it is important to evaluate LCA data critically.

Recycling

Recycling materials reduces the need to extract new raw materials, saves energy, and reduces waste going to landfill. Factors affecting recycling decisions include: the cost of collection and processing, the value of the recycled material, the energy savings compared to making new material, and public willingness to recycle. Metals such as aluminium are particularly worth recycling because extracting aluminium from bauxite by electrolysis is very energy-intensive — recycling aluminium uses only about 5% of the energy needed to extract it from ore. Glass, paper and many plastics can also be recycled, though the economics depend on collection costs, sorting complexity and the market value of recycled material.

Crude Oil and Hydrocarbons

Crude oil is a finite resource and a vital feedstock for the petrochemical industry. It is a complex mixture of hundreds of different hydrocarbons — mostly alkanes, which have the general formula \(C_nH_{2n+2}\). Crude oil is separated into useful fractions by fractional distillation. The oil is heated and vapours rise up a fractionating column; fractions with lower boiling points (shorter molecules with weaker intermolecular forces) are collected near the top, and those with higher boiling points (longer molecules with stronger intermolecular forces) near the bottom. The main fractions include refinery gases, petrol (gasoline), kerosene, diesel, fuel oil and bitumen.

Cracking breaks long-chain hydrocarbons (which are less useful) into shorter, more useful molecules. There is high demand for short-chain hydrocarbons (for fuels) and for alkenes (used to make polymers). Cracking can be done by passing hydrocarbon vapour over a hot catalyst (catalytic cracking) or by mixing with steam at very high temperatures (steam cracking). The products include shorter alkanes (used as fuels like petrol and diesel) and alkenes (unsaturated hydrocarbons used as the starting materials for making polymers such as polyethylene and polypropylene). The general equation for cracking might look like: \(C_{10}H_{22} \rightarrow C_8H_{18} + C_2H_4\), where a long-chain alkane is split into a shorter alkane and an alkene.

Key Fact

Crude oil is a finite resource and a vital feedstock for the petrochemical industry. It is separated by fractional distillation based on boiling point. Long-chain hydrocarbons are cracked to produce shorter, more useful alkanes (fuels) and alkenes (for making polymers). Modern life is crucially dependent on hydrocarbons for energy, transport and materials.

before.content_html:
Finite and Renewable Resources

The Earth provides natural resources that humans depend on. Finite resources (also called non-renewable) will eventually run out because they are consumed faster than they form. Examples include fossil fuels (coal, oil, natural gas), which took millions of years to form from the remains of ancient organisms, and metal ores mined from the Earth’s crust. Renewable resources can be replaced at the same rate they are used — examples include wood (from managed forests), crops, wind energy, solar energy and hydroelectric power.

Sustainable development means meeting the needs of the current population without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs. This requires careful management of resources, reducing waste, recycling materials, developing alternatives to finite resources, and ensuring that the environmental costs of production are minimised at every stage. Chemistry plays a central role in sustainable development — from designing industrial processes with higher atom economy and lower waste to developing biodegradable materials, more efficient batteries, and renewable energy technologies such as hydrogen fuel cells.

Key Fact

Sustainable development requires using resources wisely so that future generations can meet their needs. This involves reducing consumption of finite resources, recycling, and developing renewable alternatives.

Potable Water

Potable water is water that is safe to drink. It is not pure in the chemical sense (it still contains dissolved substances such as mineral salts) but has sufficiently low levels of dissolved salts and harmful microbes to be safe for human consumption. The UK is fortunate to have abundant fresh water from rivers, lakes and reservoirs. Potable water is produced from these sources by a multi-stage process that involves:

Step 1: Filtration — passing the water through filter beds (sand and gravel) to remove solid particles and debris. Step 2: Sterilisation — killing harmful bacteria and microorganisms. This can be done using chlorine, ozone or ultraviolet (UV) light. Chlorine is most commonly used in the UK because it is effective, cheap, and continues to kill bacteria as the water travels through the distribution network.

In areas with limited fresh water, sea water or brackish water (slightly salty water) can be made potable by desalination. This can be done by distillation (boiling and condensing) or by reverse osmosis (forcing water through a membrane that blocks dissolved salts). Desalination requires large amounts of energy, making it expensive. In the UK, where rainfall is generally sufficient, fresh water treatment is more cost-effective. In arid countries like Saudi Arabia or the UAE, desalination is essential despite the high energy cost.

Treating Waste Water

Waste water (from homes, industry and agriculture) must be treated before being released back into the environment. Sewage treatment is a multi-stage process: screening and grit removal (removing large solids and debris), primary sedimentation (allowing smaller solids to settle as sludge in settlement tanks), biological treatment (aerobic microorganisms break down dissolved organic matter in aeration tanks), secondary sedimentation, and final filtration and sterilisation before the clean effluent is returned to rivers. Industrial waste water may also contain harmful chemicals such as heavy metals or toxic organic compounds that require specialised treatment before the water can be safely released. Agricultural run-off containing fertilisers can cause eutrophication in waterways if not properly managed.

Atmospheric Pollutants

The combustion of fossil fuels produces several harmful pollutants that damage human health and the environment. You need to know the source, identity and effects of each one:

Carbon monoxide (CO) — produced by incomplete combustion of fuels. It is a toxic, colourless, odourless gas that reduces the blood’s ability to carry oxygen by binding to haemoglobin. Sulfur dioxide (\(SO_2\)) — produced when fossil fuels containing sulfur impurities are burned. It causes acid rain, which damages buildings, harms aquatic life and kills plants. Oxides of nitrogen (\(NO_x\)) — produced at high temperatures in car engines when nitrogen and oxygen from the air react. They also cause acid rain and contribute to smog. Particulates (tiny solid particles, including soot) — produced by incomplete combustion. They cause respiratory problems, reduced visibility, and can contribute to climate change.

Key Fact

Burning fossil fuels produces: carbon monoxide (toxic gas, incomplete combustion), sulfur dioxide (acid rain), oxides of nitrogen (acid rain, smog), and particulates (respiratory problems). These pollutants have serious health and environmental impacts.

Reducing Pollution

Pollution from combustion can be reduced by: using catalytic converters in vehicles (which convert CO and \(NO_x\) to less harmful \(CO_2\) and \(N_2\)), removing sulfur from fuels before burning, using flue gas desulfurisation in power stations, switching to renewable energy sources, and improving engine efficiency. Switching to electric vehicles reduces exhaust emissions at the point of use, though the overall environmental benefit depends on how the electricity is generated. These strategies involve balancing environmental benefits against economic costs technological feasibility, and public willingness to change behaviour.
